title: Characterising Intergroup Bias: Stereotyping, Prejudice and Discrimination
summary: The three faces of intergroup bias, how they differ as thought, feeling and action, and why each can appear without the others.

lesson.title: Judging before knowing
lesson.hook: 'Don't rent your flat to students, they never pay.' The landlord has never met you. What exactly is going on in their head, and in their heart?

slides.heading: Prejudice is a pre-judgement
slides.body:
**Prejudice** is a negative attitude towards a group and its members, formed **without enough information** and **resistant to evidence** that contradicts it.

The word itself tells the story: *pre*-judge. The verdict comes before the facts. Show the prejudiced person a counter-example and they often call it 'the exception', keeping the original view intact.

slides.heading: More than an opinion
slides.body:
In psychology, prejudice is not just a belief like 'they are lazy'. It is an **attitude**, and attitudes carry **feelings**: contempt, dislike, fear, even loathing.

That emotional charge is what makes prejudice so stubborn and so dangerous. Extreme cases, such as calls to kill a whole national or religious group, show how hatred of a category can override any judgement of individuals.

left.title: Explicit
points: Openly stated
Made public in words
Person is aware of it

right.title: Implicit
points: Unspoken
May be outside awareness
Shows in quick reactions

slides.question: A man insists he treats all ethnic groups equally, yet he reacts faster when pairing one group with negative words. This suggests:
slides.why: Bias that is unspoken and may lie outside awareness is implicit. Explicit prejudice is openly stated, which he denies.

slides.heading: Where 'stereotype' came from
slides.body:
The word began in **printing**. Around 1798 the French printer **Didot** used it for a metal plate that made identical copies again and again.

In 1922 the journalist **Walter Lippmann** borrowed it for '**pictures in our heads**': fixed mental copies of what a group is like. The image fits: a stereotype stamps the same impression onto every member, whoever they actually are.

slides.heading: Generalising about groups
slides.body:
A **stereotype** is a generalisation, often an **over-generalisation**, about the members of a group. Stereotypes can be **positive** ('they are great at business') as well as negative, though most are negative and **resist change**.

On their own, stereotypes are beliefs. Their harm comes from what they feed: prejudice and discrimination.

slides.heading: The 'smart tribe' stereotype
slides.story: In Chinedu's class, people joke that students from one state 'are all born engineers'. It sounds like praise. But when Musa from that state struggles in calculus, classmates assume he is lazy rather than offering help, and a lecturer expects top marks he cannot yet deliver.
slides.takeaway: Even a positive stereotype is an over-generalisation that can hurt the individual it is pinned on.

slides.question: Lippmann's description of stereotypes as 'pictures in our heads' highlights that stereotypes are:
options: Fixed mental images of a group
slides.why: The phrase stresses that stereotypes are mental copies of a group. Unfair treatment is discrimination, a behaviour.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect definitions dressed up as fill-in-the-gap: 'a set of negative attitudes formed without sufficient information and resistant to contrary evidence is…'. The trap is choosing stereotype. Remember: prejudice is the attitude with feeling; stereotype is the generalisation. Also know who coined the term and the implicit versus explicit split.
slides.sampleQuestion: The term 'stereotype' was first used by: (a) Lippmann for a mental image (b) Didot for a printing process (c) Allport for prejudice (d) Tajfel for social categories
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (b): Didot, a French printer, around 1798. Lippmann later applied it to 'pictures in our heads' in 1922.

points: Prejudice: a negative attitude formed without enough information, resistant to evidence.
Prejudice includes feelings such as contempt and loathing.
Explicit prejudice is stated; implicit prejudice is unspoken or unconscious.
'Stereotype' came from printing (Didot, 1798); Lippmann: pictures in our heads.
Stereotypes are over-generalisations, positive or negative.

questions.stem: A negative attitude towards a group, formed without enough information and resistant to contrary evidence, is:
questions.explanation: That is the standard description of prejudice. A stereotype is a generalisation; discrimination is behaviour.

questions.stem: The term 'stereotype' was originally used in:
questions.explanation: It began as a printing process for making identical copies, used by the French printer Didot.

questions.stem: Prejudice that is openly stated is called:
questions.explanation: Explicit prejudice is verbalised and made public. Implicit prejudice stays unspoken.

questions.stem: Which of the following is TRUE of stereotypes?
options: They are a form of behaviour
They can be positive or negative
questions.explanation: Stereotypes can be positive or negative, though most are negative. They are beliefs, not behaviour.

questions.stem: In psychology, prejudice is treated as an attitude rather than a mere opinion because it includes:
options: Feelings such as contempt or dislike
questions.explanation: Attitudes carry emotional content. Prejudice involves feelings like contempt, which opinions alone need not have.

questions.stem: The phrase 'pictures in our heads' is associated with:
questions.explanation: Lippmann (1922) used the phrase for stereotypes. Didot used the word only for printing.

questions.stem: Amaka says 'Northerners are very honest' about every northerner she meets. Her belief is best described as:
questions.explanation: It is a generalisation about a whole group, so a stereotype, and a positive one. No unfair treatment is described, so it is not discrimination.

questions.stem: A landlord refuses to believe a student tenant who has paid on time for two years is reliable, calling him 'the exception'. This shows prejudice is:
questions.explanation: Dismissing contrary evidence as an exception is the classic way prejudice resists change.

questions.stem: A participant denies any bias but is slower to link a minority group with positive words in a reaction-time test. The bias revealed is:
questions.explanation: Unspoken bias that shows in quick reactions, possibly outside awareness, is implicit prejudice.

questions.stem: All of the following describe prejudice EXCEPT:
options: It is the unfair treatment of group members
It can include feelings of loathing
questions.explanation: Unfair treatment is discrimination, a behaviour. Prejudice is the attitude behind it.

questions.stem: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: Implicit prejudice: may be outside awareness
questions.explanation: Implicit prejudice can lie outside awareness. Explicit prejudice is conscious and stated; generalisation is a stereotype; unfair behaviour is discrimination.

questions.stem: Why are stereotypes described as harmful even though they are 'only beliefs'?
questions.explanation: Their danger lies in what they feed: hostile feelings and unfair treatment. They are not always false, and they resist change.

questions.stem: I. Prejudice includes an emotional component. II. Stereotypes are always negative. III. Implicit prejudice may operate outside awareness. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and III are correct. II is wrong because stereotypes can be positive.

questions.stem: A researcher shows that a group's stereotype persists even after members are shown many disconfirming cases. The researcher would most likely conclude that stereotypes:
questions.explanation: Survival in the face of contrary evidence shows resistance to change. If facts dissolved stereotypes, they would have disappeared.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the relationship between stereotypes and prejudice?
options: Stereotypes are beliefs that can fuel prejudiced attitudes
Prejudice always comes before any stereotype
Stereotypes are feelings and prejudice is behaviour
questions.explanation: Stereotypes are the generalised beliefs; prejudice is the negative attitude they often feed. Behaviour is discrimination.

lesson.title: From thinking to doing
lesson.hook: A hiring manager says he has nothing against anyone, yet every new staff member is from his hometown. Is that discrimination if there is no hatred behind it?

slides.heading: Discrimination is behaviour
slides.body:
**Discrimination** is treating people differently, usually worse, **because of the group they belong to**. It puts members of a group at a disadvantage.

Where a stereotype lives in the head and prejudice in the heart, discrimination shows in the **hands**: who gets hired, admitted, served, promoted or rented a flat.

steps.title: Stereotype (thinking)
steps.detail: The cognitive part: a generalised belief about what group members are like.

steps.title: Prejudice (feeling)
steps.detail: The emotional part: a negative attitude such as dislike or contempt.

steps.title: Discrimination (doing)
steps.detail: The behavioural part: unequal treatment because of group membership.

slides.question: Which of these is discrimination rather than prejudice or stereotype?
options: Refusing to serve customers of a group
slides.why: Discrimination is an action. Believing and imagining are stereotypes; disliking is prejudice.

left.title: Personal
points: Committed by individuals
A manager won't hire a Hausa applicant
A trader overcharges one group

right.title: Institutional
points: Built into policies and practices
Admission rules favouring one ethnic group
Can continue without any one bigot

slides.heading: The admission rule
slides.story: A private college quietly reserves most places for applicants from its founder's home area. No single admissions officer dislikes anyone; they are just following the rule. Yet year after year, equally qualified students like Zainab from other states are turned away.
slides.takeaway: Institutional discrimination is built into rules and practices, so it can harm people even when no individual feels hatred.

slides.heading: Love for 'us', not hate for 'them'
slides.body:
**Marilynn Brewer (1999)** argued that much discrimination grows from **in-group favouritism** rather than hostility towards the out-group.

The manager who hires only people from his hometown may feel no hatred for anyone else. He simply trusts and helps 'his own'. The result for outsiders is the same: fewer chances. Brewer's question became famous: is prejudice **in-group love or out-group hate**?

slides.heading: They do not always travel together
slides.body:
Stereotype, prejudice and discrimination often go together, but **one can exist without the others**.

Someone can dislike 'foreigners' in general without holding specific stereotypes or ever acting on it. And discrimination can happen **without prejudice**, intentionally or not, as when a rule or habit disadvantages a group nobody set out to harm. In a classic 1930s study, **Richard LaPiere** found hotels that served a Chinese couple in person later said in letters they would refuse Chinese guests: attitudes and actions did not match.

slides.question: A hospital form that only accepts names in one language, unintentionally excluding some patients, is an example of:
slides.why: The rule disadvantages a group though nobody intended harm. That shows discrimination can occur without prejudice.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: The favourite is 'differentiate between stereotype, prejudice and discrimination'. Use the thinking, feeling, doing frame and give one example of each. Objectives test personal versus institutional discrimination with Nigerian scenarios, and whether discrimination can exist without prejudice. The trap: assuming discrimination always needs hatred.
slides.sampleQuestion: A university's quota system admits fewer candidates from some states regardless of their scores. This is best described as: (a) personal discrimination (b) institutional discrimination (c) implicit prejudice (d) a stereotype
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (b): it is a policy carried out by an institution, not an act by one individual. In essays, explain that it can exist even if no officer is prejudiced.

points: Discrimination is unequal treatment because of group membership.
Stereotype = thinking, prejudice = feeling, discrimination = doing.
Personal discrimination: individuals; institutional: policies and practices.
Brewer (1999): much discrimination is in-group love, not out-group hate.
Each of the three can occur without the others.

questions.stem: Discrimination is best defined as:
options: Unequal treatment of people because of their group
A negative feeling towards a group
questions.explanation: Discrimination is behaviour: treating people differently because of group membership. Beliefs are stereotypes; feelings are prejudice.

questions.stem: Discrimination committed by an individual person is called:
questions.explanation: Acts by individuals are personal discrimination. Policies of organisations are institutional discrimination.

questions.stem: Which component of intergroup bias is behavioural?
questions.explanation: Discrimination is the action; stereotypes are thoughts and prejudice is a feeling-laden attitude.

questions.stem: Brewer (1999) argued that much discrimination stems from:
questions.explanation: Brewer stressed in-group love: helping one's own group can disadvantage others without hatred.

questions.stem: Institutional discrimination refers to:
options: Discriminatory policies or practices of organisations
questions.explanation: It is built into organisational rules and practices, unlike personal discrimination by individuals.

questions.stem: Which statement is TRUE?
options: Stereotypes are a form of behaviour
questions.explanation: Rules or habits can disadvantage a group without anyone feeling prejudice. The other statements overstate the links.

questions.stem: A shop owner in Kano refuses to employ any applicant from a particular ethnic group. This is:
questions.explanation: An individual's own act of unequal treatment is personal discrimination.

questions.stem: A state civil service rule gives automatic promotion priority to 'indigenes', disadvantaging equally qualified non-indigenes. This is:
questions.explanation: The disadvantage comes from an organisational policy, which is institutional discrimination.

questions.stem: A manager always hires people from his own church, not because he dislikes others but because he trusts members. Brewer would describe this as:
questions.explanation: Favouring one's own without hostility to others is the in-group love Brewer described. The effect on outsiders is still discriminatory.

questions.stem: LaPiere's 1930s study, in which hotels served a Chinese couple but later said they would refuse Chinese guests, shows that:
options: Stated attitudes and actual behaviour can differ
questions.explanation: The gap between the letters and the actual service shows attitude and behaviour can come apart.

questions.stem: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.explanation: Prejudice is the feeling component. Stereotypes are cognitive, discrimination behavioural, and institutional discrimination works through policies.

questions.stem: All of the following are examples of discrimination EXCEPT:
options: Privately believing a group is untidy
Promoting staff only from one region
questions.explanation: A private belief is a stereotype, not behaviour. The others are unequal treatment.

questions.stem: I. Discrimination can exist without prejudice. II. Prejudice can exist without specific stereotypes. III. Institutional discrimination needs a prejudiced individual to operate. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and II are correct. III is false: institutional discrimination can continue through rules even if no individual is prejudiced.

questions.stem: A researcher finds a company disadvantages women in promotion, yet every manager scores low on prejudice. The best explanation is:
options: Institutional discrimination built into company practices
questions.explanation: Discrimination without prejudiced individuals points to policies and practices, which is institutional discrimination. Assuming lies ignores the possibility the theory describes.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why Brewer's work matters for reducing discrimination?
options: Discrimination ends once stereotypes are positive
Only laws against hate speech are needed
Removing hatred alone may not end discrimination if in-group favouritism remains
questions.explanation: If discrimination often flows from favouring one's own, then reducing hostility is not enough; favouritism must be tackled too.
